## What Is a Time Series?

::: two-col
<div>

A **time series** is a sequence of values recorded at regular points in
time --- hourly, daily, monthly.

What makes it different from a normal table: **order matters.** Monday
connects to Tuesday. Shuffling the rows destroys the information.

::: {style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:8px;margin-top:10px;"}
::: {.card .card-teal style="padding:10px 12px;"}
::: {style="font-size:1.2em;margin-bottom:3px;"}
📅
:::

**Timestamp**\
[When a visit, click, or campaign event
happened.]{style="font-size:0.82em;color:#94A3B8;"}
:::

::: {.card .card-orange style="padding:10px 12px;"}
::: {style="font-size:1.2em;margin-bottom:3px;"}
📏
:::

**Value**\
[The metric measured at that
moment.]{style="font-size:0.82em;color:#94A3B8;"}
:::
:::

::: info
💡 **Our example:** Stock market daily changes, 2018--2022. COVID-19
creates a clear "before, during, after" --- perfect for seeing every
concept.
:::

::: slide-summary
In marketing analytics, time series helps you answer:

-   Is traffic or campaign performance trending up or down?
-   Is the behavior stable enough to make reliable forecasts?
:::

</div>

## Concept 1 --- Trend & Stationarity

::: two-col
### 📈 Trend --- the Long-Run Direction

The **trend** is the overall direction after smoothing noise. We use a
**rolling mean** --- averaging the last N observations as we slide along
the series.

::: {#5ca81f6f .cell execution_count="3"}
::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
<div>

<figure>
<p><img src="ms4_files/figure-2.png" role="img" width="744"
height="368" /></p>
</figure>

</div>
:::
:::

::: info
The navy line removes noise --- now **up → crash → recover** is obvious.
:::

### 🔄 Stationarity --- Does It Stay Consistent?

A series is **stationary** when its average and spread stay roughly
stable over time. Most analysis tools require this. Raw prices drift up
forever --- not stationary. Daily % changes bounce near zero ---
stationary.

::: {#d748d882 .cell execution_count="4"}
::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
<div>

<figure>
<p><img src="ms4_files/figure-3.png" role="img" width="744"
height="395" /></p>
</figure>

</div>
:::
:::

::: dark
**Fix:** Use daily % change instead of the raw price level.
:::
:::
:::

## Concept 2 --- Rolling Windows & Volatility

::: two-col
<div>

### 🪟 Rolling Windows

A rolling window slides along the series recomputing a statistic using
only the **most recent N days.** This turns a single number into a
**story over time.**

::: step
::: step-n
1
:::

::: step-b
#### Pick window size (e.g. 30 days)

How far back do you want to look?
:::
:::

::: step
::: step-n
2
:::

::: step-b
#### Compute mean or std dev

For just those N days
:::
:::

::: step
::: step-n
3
:::

::: step-b
#### Slide forward one day, repeat

You now have a value for every date
:::
:::

### 📊 Volatility = Rolling Std Dev

**Volatility** = how much the series jumps around. Computed as the
rolling standard deviation of daily changes.

::: warn
⚡ Rolling windows show **when** the series changed --- not just that it
changed.
:::

</div>

## Concept 3 --- Structural Break

A **structural break** is when the series **permanently shifts** its
behaviour at a specific point. Models trained before the break give
wrong answers after it.

::: two-col
<div>

::: {#86e79a99 .cell execution_count="6"}
::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
<div>

<figure>
<p><img src="ms4_files/figure-5.png" role="img" width="796"
height="511" /></p>
</figure>

</div>
:::
:::

</div>

<div>

::: {.card .card-orange style="margin-bottom:10px;"}
### 🎂 The Recipe Analogy

You are baking a cake. Everything works fine for 6 steps. Then at step
7, someone **swaps sugar for salt** --- and tells nobody. Every step
after that tastes wrong. Your old model of "this is correct" is now
broken --- because the underlying process permanently changed.\
\
A structural break is exactly that swap, happening in your data.
:::

::: {.card .card-teal}
### 🔍 How to confirm a break

Compare the **mean and std dev** on each side of the suspected point. If
they differ significantly --- and the change persists --- it is a
structural break.\
\
In our data: volatility went from **\~0.77% → \~1.45% per day** and
*never returned* to the old level.
:::

::: dark
Any model built on pre-COVID data now **underestimates risk** in the
post-COVID world.
:::

</div>
:::
:::

## Concept 4 --- Signal, Momentum & Anomaly Checks

::: two-col
### 🔁 Autocorrelation --- marketing momentum {#autocorrelation-does-the-past-predict-the-future}

**Autocorrelation** measures whether today's result still reflects
yesterday's performance. In marketing, this helps identify sustained
campaign momentum rather than one-off noise.

::: info
If website traffic is high after an email blast, and the next day stays
strong too, that means the series has momentum.
:::

::: {#3c37654e .cell execution_count="7"}
::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
<div>

<figure>
<p><img src="ms4_files/figure-6.png" role="img" width="766"
height="390" /></p>
</figure>

</div>
:::
:::

::: info
During COVID, **lag-1 is significant** --- panic had momentum. One bad
day predicted the next. Before and after: more random, less memory.
:::

### 🚨 Anomaly Detection --- 3-Sigma Rule

Flag any point more than **3 standard deviations** from the mean. In
normal data only 0.3% of points qualify --- so anything flagged is
genuinely unusual.

::: {.formula style="font-size:0.88em;"}
Flag if: \|value − mean\| \> 3 × std dev
:::

::: {#4a921f92 .cell execution_count="8"}
::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
<div>

<figure>
<p><img src="ms4_files/figure-7.png" role="img" width="770"
height="407" /></p>
</figure>

</div>
:::
:::

::: warn
⚡ In marketing terms, these anomalies are sudden shifts from normal
behavior --- like campaign spikes or pandemic-driven traffic shocks.
They flag when your model is no longer capturing the true signal.
:::
:::
:::

## Key Takeaways

::: slide-summary
-   Marketing time series are ordered signals --- sequence matters.
-   Use changes or percentage returns to compare campaigns fairly.
-   Detect shifts early with rolling measures and break analysis.
-   Adapt models when structural breaks or anomalies appear.
:::

::: final-note
💡

Use these concepts to spot meaningful patterns quickly: stable changes,
regime shifts, momentum, and true anomalies. The same approach applies
to any time-driven dataset, not just markets.
:::
:::
